title: "Talent Is Universal, Opportunity Is Not": Wadhwani Foundation CEO Dr. Ajay Kela on Why the Diaspora's Greatest Asset Isn't Money
excerpt: In an exclusive interview with The Videshi, the CEO of Wadhwani Foundation talks about India's innovation ecosystem, the "missing middle" of Indian entrepreneurship, and why the diaspora's most powerful currency isn't capital — it's knowledge.
body:
• The diaspora's greatest assets are knowledge, networks, and experience — not financial capital
  • India's "missing middle" — growth-stage companies in tier-2 and tier-3 cities — represents a massive untapped opportunity for impact
  • India doesn't have a research problem; it has a translation problem — turning lab discoveries into products and companies
  • The next generation of globally significant deep-tech companies will increasingly be built in India, for the world

Every year, thousands of accomplished Indians abroad talk about "giving back" to India. Most never get past the talking. Dr. Ajay Kela actually did it — walking away from a successful corporate career in the United States to lead the Wadhwani Foundation, one of the most ambitious development organizations working in India today.

Founded in 2001 by Silicon Valley entrepreneur and Padma Shri awardee Dr. Romesh Wadhwani, the Foundation operates at a scale that few non-profits attempt: a mission to create 5 million jobs and upskill 25 million people by 2030, working across entrepreneurship, skilling, innovation, and government digital transformation. Its Wadhwani Innovation Network partners with institutions including IISc Bangalore, IIT Bombay, IIT Kanpur, IIT Madras, and C-CAMP to turn world-class research into startups and commercially viable products — bridging the gap between India's laboratories and its markets.

In this exclusive interview with The Videshi, Dr. Kela speaks candidly about what it actually takes to give back meaningfully, why India's biggest entrepreneurial opportunity lies outside its metros, and what the diaspora gets wrong about impact.

On leaving a corporate career for impact

The Videshi: You had a successful career in the US. What was the specific moment or realization that made you decide to shift from building wealth to building impact in India?

Dr. Kela: It wasn't one defining moment, rather a series of experiences that began in my childhood. I grew up in a 350-square-foot apartment with a family of six before a sponsored education took me to the United States. That opportunity changed the trajectory of an entire generation of my family. It taught me that one opportunity, at the right time, can create ripple effects that last for decades.

Over the years, I saw that same pattern repeat itself. My driver, Deepak, was bright and hardworking. I encouraged him to earn networking certifications. While I worked in my office, he sat in the parking lot with a borrowed laptop, studying while he waited for me to finish work. A few certifications and one job referral later, his career took off. Today, his children enjoy opportunities comparable to those of my own.

Then there was Chandu, my cook. I encouraged him to start catering community events while he worked for our family. Word spread, his side-gig flourished, he went on to cater weddings and large events across Mumbai, and today he runs his own restaurant.

Three very different people. One common lesson: talent is universal; opportunity is not.

When the opportunity arose for me to lead the Wadhwani Foundation, it felt like the natural culmination of everything I had learned. Instead of changing one life at a time, I could help build systems that create opportunity for millions. Today, our mission is to help create 5 million jobs and enable 25 million people to earn family-sustaining wages through entrepreneurship, skilling, innovation, and government transformation. That is simply scaling the same lesson I learned from Deepak and Chandu: change one life, and you often change many more.

"Talent is universal; opportunity is not."

On why NRIs struggle to give back — and how to start

The Videshi: There are thousands of accomplished NRIs who talk about "giving back" but never do it. What actually stops them — and what would you tell a 35-year-old Indian-American engineer in Silicon Valley who wants to start but doesn't know how?

Dr. Kela: I think one of the biggest misconceptions is that giving back begins with writing a large cheque. For most members of the diaspora, the greatest assets are not financial — instead they are knowledge, networks, credibility, and experience accumulated over decades.

A young engineer in Silicon Valley can mentor a startup founder in Jaipur, introduce an AI researcher at IISc to a potential collaborator, advise a deep-tech company on product strategy, or help a student prepare for an international career. Those contributions can be as valuable as funding.

What India needs today is institution builders. That means helping create mentorship networks, strengthen research ecosystems, open doors for entrepreneurs, connect academia with industry, and share global best practices.

At Wadhwani Foundation, we've seen how partnerships between governments, universities, entrepreneurs, industry, and the diaspora can create impact at national scale. The diaspora is uniquely positioned to bridge these worlds because it understands both India and the global innovation ecosystem.

So, my advice is simple: Don't wait until you think you've "made it." Start with what you already know, who you already know, and whom you can already help. The most meaningful legacy is rarely what you donate; it's what you help build.

On India's "missing middle" beyond the metros

The Videshi: You've said the Foundation wants to reach founders beyond IITs and metros. What does that look like in practice? Who are you finding in tier-2 and tier-3 India that the ecosystem is overlooking?

Dr. Kela: One of the biggest myths in entrepreneurship is that innovation happens only in Bengaluru, Gurgaon, or Hyderabad. Some of the most impressive entrepreneurs I meet run manufacturing businesses in Kanpur, build agri-solutions in Surat, create healthcare innovations in Coimbatore, or solve local problems in dozens of other cities across India.

These founders understand their customers deeply because they live alongside them. They've built resilient businesses, often with limited resources, and many are already creating jobs in their communities. What they usually lack isn't talent or ambition — but access. Access to experienced mentors who have scaled companies before. Access to AI tools and technology expertise. Access to customers, investors, strategic partners, and growth networks.

These businesses are what we call India's "missing middle." They are beyond the startup stage — they have paying customers and proven products — but they are still too small to attract major consulting firms or growth investors.

That's precisely where Wadhwani Accelerate focuses. We help growth-stage companies strengthen execution, adopt AI, scale faster, and create more jobs. In 2025 alone, the Foundation supported 7,000 businesses, demonstrating that with the right ecosystem, entrepreneurs outside traditional startup hubs can scale just as successfully.

The future of Indian entrepreneurship won't be built in five cities. It will be built across hundreds of cities where talent has always existed but opportunity has not.

On India's lab-to-market problem

The Videshi: India produces world-class research but struggles to commercialize it. What's actually broken in the lab-to-market pipeline, and how is the Innovation Centre at IISc designed to fix it?

Dr. Kela: India doesn't have a research problem — it has a translation problem. Our universities and research institutions produce outstanding science, patents, and breakthrough discoveries. Yet only a small fraction ever becomes products, companies, or technologies that improve people's lives.

Researchers are trained to solve scientific problems. Bringing those discoveries to market requires a completely different set of capabilities — market validation, product development, IP strategy, regulatory navigation, fundraising, entrepreneurship, and industry partnerships.

I often say that India isn't short of gold mines of innovation; we're short of the machinery that turns gold into products.

The Wadhwani Innovation Network works with institutions such as IISc, IIT Bombay, IIT Kanpur, IIT Madras, C-CAMP, and others to create a complete innovation pipeline — from research translation to startup creation and commercialization.

The Wadhwani-IISc Innovation Centre isn't simply another research centre; it's a translation engine. Success won't be measured by papers published or patents filed, but by startups launched, products commercialized, industries strengthened, and societal problems solved.

"India isn't short of gold mines of innovation; we're short of the machinery that turns gold into products."

On what Indian students in the US need to hear

The Videshi: If you could put one message in front of every Indian student currently in a US university, what would it be?

Dr. Kela: Learn, grow, and dream big. A global education is one of the greatest gifts you can receive.

But I'd also tell every student this: Don't confuse staying abroad with succeeding. The India many of us left behind no longer exists. Today, India is one of the world's fastest-growing innovation ecosystems. Whether it's AI, deep tech, manufacturing, biotech, clean energy, digital public infrastructure, or entrepreneurship — there are opportunities to build at a scale very few countries can match.

Success isn't measured only by your salary, title, or ZIP code. It's measured by the problems you solve, the opportunities you create for others, and the institutions you help build.

My advice: go wherever you can learn the most. Build global expertise. Create international networks. But at some point, ask yourself one important question — where can I have the greatest impact? For an increasing number of people, the answer is India.

On the deep-tech opportunity for the diaspora

The Videshi: The Wadhwani Innovation Network is placing bets on deep-tech at institutions like IISc. For diaspora professionals in quantum, AI, or biotech — what does the opportunity look like right now to build something meaningful in India that they couldn't build abroad?

Dr. Kela: Twenty years ago, if you wanted to build a frontier technology company, India probably wasn't your first choice. Today, that equation has changed dramatically.

India offers a rare combination of world-class technical talent, outstanding research institutions, strong government commitment, entrepreneurial energy, and perhaps most importantly — enormous market scale. Few countries allow you to develop technologies that can improve the lives of hundreds of millions of people while simultaneously building globally competitive companies.

What makes this moment unique is the convergence of multiple forces: increased public investment through initiatives such as the IndiaAI Mission, the National Quantum Mission, the establishment of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation, growing private-sector investment, and innovation platforms like the Wadhwani Innovation Network.

For diaspora professionals, the opportunity extends far beyond relocating. You can mentor research teams, co-found deep-tech startups, advise translational research, invest in emerging companies, collaborate with universities, or help Indian innovations access global markets.

I believe the next generation of globally significant deep-tech companies won't simply be built for India. They'll increasingly be built in India, for the world.

On redirecting diaspora capital

The Videshi: Diaspora capital tends to flow to familiar patterns — IIT founders, English-speaking teams, Bangalore and Mumbai. How do you redirect that capital to less obvious but equally deserving founders?

Dr. Kela: Capital follows confidence. Investors naturally gravitate toward ecosystems they understand. The answer isn't to ask them to take more risk, but to reduce perceived risk by building stronger regional ecosystems with mentors, industry connections, market access, and commercialization support.

We also need to broaden our definition of a high-potential founder. Some of the best entrepreneurs work closest to the problems — whether in agriculture, manufacturing, healthcare, or energy — and bring invaluable contextual understanding.

As these ecosystems mature, capital will increasingly follow talent and opportunity rather than geography.

On measuring success differently

The Videshi: You've spent decades optimizing for revenue growth. How do you measure success now? What metric keeps you up at night?

Dr. Kela: In business, revenue is a clear measure of value creation. At Wadhwani Foundation, the metrics are: jobs created, students placed in decent jobs, businesses supported, students made job-ready, startups launched, and research translated.

But the question I keep coming back to is simpler: Did we meaningfully change someone's trajectory? Did a student gain access to a better career? Did an entrepreneur create more jobs? Did a research breakthrough reach society at scale?

What keeps me up at night is speed. Are we creating opportunity fast enough to match the scale of the challenge — a rapidly growing youth population in India, Africa, Indonesia, Brazil, and other countries? The faster we can move people from potential to meaningful outcomes, the greater our impact.

On what the government is getting right — and wrong

The Videshi: What's one thing the Indian government is getting right about deep-tech and innovation policy — and one thing they're getting wrong?

Dr. Kela: The government deserves significant credit for recognizing that deep-tech requires patient capital and long-term institutional support. The National Quantum Mission, IndiaAI Mission, and Anusandhan National Research Foundation are important steps toward strengthening India's research and innovation ecosystem.

The next challenge is commercialization. India is getting better at funding research and early-stage innovation, but too many promising technologies struggle to reach the market. Often, startups don't need another grant — but a first customer.

Government and industry can play a much greater role as early adopters, supported by stronger translational funding and technology-transfer mechanisms. India's next innovation chapter will be defined not by how much research we produce, but by how much of it becomes products, companies, jobs, and societal impact.

On what real success looks like in five years

The Videshi: Five years from now, what does success look like for the Wadhwani-IISc Innovation Centre — not in press releases, but in real outcomes?

Dr. Kela: Success won't be measured by projects funded or patents filed. It will be measured by discoveries becoming products, products becoming companies, and those companies solving meaningful problems at scale.

I would like to see startups emerging from the Centre that have raised independent capital, secured customers, built globally competitive technologies, and created measurable impact across areas such as AI, quantum technologies, healthcare, advanced materials, and clean energy.

The deeper measure, however, is cultural: have we made commercialization a natural extension of world-class research?

If IISc can demonstrate a repeatable model for translating research into companies and societal impact, it can be replicated across India. Ultimately, the strongest measure of success is whether we build an ecosystem that continues to thrive without us.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Wadhwani Foundation, founded in 2001 by Padma Shri Dr. Romesh Wadhwani, works across entrepreneurship, skilling, innovation, and government digital transformation in emerging economies. Learn more at wadhwanifoundation.org.
